strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing genuine LLM limitations by leveraging structured external materials for tool creation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three domains (causality, physics, chemistry) with multiple benchmarks, models, and both automatic and human evaluation
Strong and consistent results: 11.3% average improvement over existing methods, outperforming specialized domain-specific baselines
Systematic two-module design with clear hierarchical organization that naturally mirrors reference material structure
Human evaluation validates tool quality: ~90% faithful and useful tools, with good consistency between human and model selections
Significant practical efficiency gains: 97% inference time reduction and 99% cost reduction compared to specialized methods
Concrete case studies effectively demonstrate value of the approach on problems where baselines fail
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices with implementation details, prompts, evaluation protocols, and additional results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (LLM-based generation, hierarchical retrieval) without introducing fundamentally new methods
Scope restricted to knowledge-intensive quantitative reasoning tasks; unclear applicability to other domains like code generation or creative reasoning
Assumes access to well-structured reference materials; strategy for domains lacking such resources is not addressed
Requires LLMs to possess foundational domain knowledge for effective tool generation and selection; performance in unfamiliar domains unexplored
Hierarchical approach may not generalize to domains with different organizational structures than textbook-like hierarchies
Ablation study could be more comprehensive (e.g., sensitivity to prompt design, alternative hierarchical structures, different retrieval strategies)
Limited analysis of failure cases; paper focuses on successes with minimal discussion of when/why RefTool fails
Tool reusability claims demonstrated only on one additional dataset (SciBench-fund); broader generalization evidence would strengthen claims
Scalability with large reference materials not thoroughly analyzed; computational cost analysis limited to specific examples
Prompt engineering sensitivity not analyzed despite reliance on carefully designed prompts
Baseline comparisons with domain-specific methods may not be entirely fair; more comparisons with general tool-augmented reasoning methods would be informative

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach using external references to overcome LLM knowledge limitations, addressing a genuine gap in existing tool creation methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three knowledge-intensive domains (causality, physics, chemistry) with multiple datasets, baselines from four categories, and systematic generalization studies
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements: 13.0% over tool creation methods, 10.2% over domain-specific methods, with 99% cost reduction vs. ChemAgent
Thorough analysis including ablation studies (code format: 1.9%, hierarchical selection: 2.6%), human evaluation of tool quality (≥89% satisfactory), and cost-benefit analysis
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, comprehensive appendices with prompts and additional results, promise to release code and data
Tools are dataset-agnostic and reusable, with demonstrated compatibility across LLM families and successful generalization to non-scientific domains (language translation)
Clear technical soundness with logical two-stage pipeline (creation with validation, then hierarchical selection) and graceful degradation when no tools apply
weaknesses: Limited scope: only 3 textbooks across 3 scientific domains tested; textbooks are inherently well-structured, reducing evidence for messy/unstructured materials; XLR translation is sole non-scientific domain (single language pair)

Tool creation model dependency: GPT-4o achieves 82% direct validation success vs. 54% for Gemini-1.5-Pro; ~20% of weaker-model tools still filtered after refinement, raising concerns about knowledge coverage consistency

Hierarchical design not fully justified: two-level hierarchy appears arbitrary with no comparison of depth/structure alternatives; only 2.6% improvement over similarity-based retrieval is modest; LLM-constructed hierarchies for unstructured references lack quality validation
Potential data leakage: explicitly excluded one chemistry sub-dataset due to overlap with reference material, but no systematic verification that other evaluation questions don't align with textbooks

Incomplete failure analysis: human-model consistency ranges 44-90% for tool selection (especially weak in physics/chemistry) with limited investigation of failure modes; no systematic study of question types or domains where tools don't help

Tool validation limitations: relies solely on model-generated examples without verification of representativeness; pseudo-code validation for language translation is less rigorous than actual execution
Hyperparameter tuning inconsistency: grid search only performed for chemistry (nc, nt); causality and physics use defaults, raising questions about potential improvements with domain-specific tuning

Baseline fairness concerns: RAG subsection-level retrieval may not be optimal for text comparison; domain-specific baseline issues attributed to implementation rather than fundamental limitations; missing comparisons with recent 2024-2025 retrieval-augmented methods
